name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,302

clue.text: Mr Kite arranged for frog that sings

indicators.note: to arrange letters is to put them in a new order

explanation.surface: Mr Kite, from the Beatles song, organises something on behalf of a musical frog.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Mr Kite look like a Beatles title to be taken whole; the two words are just six letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Kermit the Frog is the Muppet who sings 'Rainbow Connection'.

blocks.note: ex = former, over and done with

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a task is finished and is told yes, precisely right.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark makes 'Done deed' look like a single phrase; it splits into a former thing and an action.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: exact describes something correct in every detail, with no margin of error.

clue.text: Teacher and head of year’s expertise

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A school boasts of the know-how shared by a teacher and the head of year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of year' reads as a school job title alongside the teacher, but it only supplies the first letter. The 's stands for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastery is expert skill or command of a subject.

clue.text: XI perhaps missing final in Assam, say

indicators.note: the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: an XI (eleven) is a cricket or football team
TEAM without its last letter M

explanation.surface: A cricket eleven, lacking its final match, is touring the Indian state of Assam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final' pretends to be a cup final the team misses; it is the last letter. Assam is both an Indian state and a black tea grown there.
explanation.definitionFit: Assam is a variety of tea, with 'say' marking it as an example.

clue.text: Pupils do this in absurd detail

indicators.note: absurd letters are nonsense, so they need putting in order

explanation.surface: Schoolchildren go into ridiculous detail in their homework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupils' suggests schoolchildren; they are the pupils of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The pupils of the eyes dilate, widening in dim light.

clue.text: Problem with economy not failed, rocking

explanation.surface: An economy has trouble but has not collapsed, though it is wobbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocking' pretends to describe a shaky economy; it is the signal to rearrange 'not failed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deflation, falling prices, is an economic problem.

clue.text: Language the French can put together

indicators.note: tells you to join the two pieces side by side

explanation.surface: The French are able to assemble a language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' reads as a verb; it is the noun, a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain example: the tongue of ancient Rome, still met in law, medicine and church use.

indicators.note: a ruined word has its letters wrecked and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A politician's career is ruined by an act of betrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a political scandal, and the anagram fodder is the senator himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: this is betrayal of one's own country or ruler, the gravest kind of disloyalty.

clue.text: Fall short with man’s jolly character

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its last letter

blocks.note: to man a post is to staff it

explanation.surface: A man with a jolly nature somehow fails to measure up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fall short' looks like one idiom meaning fail; it is FALL trimmed. 'Man' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Falstaff is Shakespeare's fat, merry knight, the classic jolly character.

clue.text: Affected part in it we excise

indicators.note: the answer is part of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'it', through 'we', into the start of 'excise'

explanation.surface: Someone decides to cut out the part of a text that was damaged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' first reads as damaged; it means pretentious.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee means affectedly quaint or dainty.

clue.text: Regularly sat by set, eyelid sore

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, here every other one

blocks.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone sits regularly by the television set with a sore eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' reads as a television set; it just supplies letters. The count starts from the first letter and skips one each time.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: a small inflamed lump at the edge of an eyelid, caused by an infected lash follicle.

indicators.note: spreading letters scatters them into a new order

explanation.surface: The Soviet news agency Tass has long been spreading word of Gorbachev's policy.
explanation.walkthrough: Tass was the Soviet state news agency, so the surface is fully in period.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasnost, openness, was Gorbachev's policy of greater transparency in the 1980s USSR.

blocks.note: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, a Dane

explanation.surface: A cartoon dog might wreck a performance of Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' reads as breaking; it is praise. 'Possibly' marks Scooby-Doo as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Scooby-Doo, the cartoon detective dog, belongs to that giant breed.

clue.text: Deny organisation backed limiting means of preventing erosion

indicators.note: loosely, the word has a limit, its outer D, cut away

blocks.note: DENY with its first letter D removed

explanation.surface: A body denies that it supported restrictions on coastal defences.
explanation.walkthrough: The mechanism is loose: ORG and DENY minus D run backwards. A groyne is a low wall built out into the sea to stop sand being washed away.
explanation.definitionFit: A groyne is a barrier on a beach that prevents erosion.

clue.text: Soldier out in Egypt bears standard

indicators.note: to bear is to carry, so the outer piece holds the inner

blocks.note: the words as printed, carried inside
surface padding: it only sets the soldier's posting

explanation.surface: A soldier serving abroad in Egypt carries the regimental flag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' looks like a flag; it means ordinary. The RE (Royal Engineers) surrounds the words 'out in'; 'Egypt' just sets the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something routine is standard procedure, done the usual way.

explanation.surface: Someone's native country lies a long way from any coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' suggests a homeland; it is the everyday sense of being in.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: describes places in the interior of a country, well away from the coast.

definitions.note: 'Barking' is an adjective; LUNATIC works as the adjective too.

indicators.note: barking means mad, so the letters go crazy

explanation.surface: A strange sect sets up in Barking, and people think that is crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking appears twice: first as the London district (and anagram signal), then as British slang for mad, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Barking (mad) is British slang for crazy, and a lunatic is crazy.

explanation.surface: A garden slug turns up in the evening news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slug' suggests the garden pest; it is the other slug, a bullet.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a short official statement of news, as broadcast on radio or TV.

blocks.note: read as a verb: to put a match to something, to set it alight
read as describing easy reading or entertainment, meant for fun

explanation.surface: A game played just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' reads as a contest; as a verb it means set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting a fire going is the job a match does, and light entertainment is not serious.

explanation.surface: A body part belonging to a gorilla from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the back of the neck, where a collar sits.

indicators.note: the outer piece holds the inner one

explanation.surface: The post office has intercepted a racy picture in the mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' is the British sense, cheekily rude, which is also what hot means here.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain abbreviation: short for photograph, a captured image.

indicators.note: to protect is to surround and shield

blocks.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter jet

explanation.surface: A Russian soldier guards the reputation of a ruling family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fighter' suggests a soldier; it is a warplane.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper-name example: the Chinese imperial house from 1368 to 1644, famous for its porcelain.

definitions.note: 'Like Titanic' describes a state, which the phrase AT BOTTOM fills.

blocks.note: read literally: the liner lies on the floor of the Atlantic
read as the idiom: basically, fundamentally, when all is said and done

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the Titanic was really like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like Titanic' is playful: the wreck lies at the bottom of the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: The sunken Titanic rests on the ocean floor, and the phrase is also an idiom for fundamentally, in reality.

blocks.note: read as zoology: the vampire is one species of the flying mammal
read as sport: the implement for hitting the ball in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: A vampire is spotted at a nightclub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' reads as a nightclub; it is the thing you hit a ball with.
explanation.definitionFit: The vampire bat is one kind of the flying mammal, and a cricket or baseball bat is a club.

indicators.note: caught as in caught by the ear, heard

explanation.surface: An insect, like Ringo Starr, has been caught.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beatles' name was itself a pun on beetle, so the clue turns the joke back.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain category: any insect with hard wing cases, from the largest order of insects.

indicators.note: damaged letters get knocked out of order

explanation.surface: An insurer tallies up the cost of storm damage for an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damage' at the front reads as a noun being counted; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper-name example: the second city of Arizona, in the Sonoran Desert.
